Engaging yne-allenones in tunable catalytic
silane-mediated conjugate transfer reductions †
Xiao-Yan Qin, ‡ Jia-Yin Wang,‡ Fang-Zhou Geng, Wen-Juan Hao,
 *
Shu-Jiang Tu
 * and Bo Jiang
 *
New tunable catalytic [2+2] cycloaddition/silane-mediated conjugate
transfer reductions of yne-allenones have been developed, by which
substituent-diverse cyclobutarenes with generally good yields were
selectively synthesized by adjusting Fe
–Ha n dC u–H catalytic systems.
Use of the Fe –Hs y s t e mt r i g g e r s1 , 6 - c o n j u g a t er e d u c t i o nt o
dihydrocyclobuta[a]naphthalen-4-ols whereas the Cu–H complex
enables 1,4-conjugate reduction to cyclobuta[a ]naphthalen-4(2H)-
ones.
As a class of highly strained carbocycles, cyclobutarenes show a
wide spectrum of biological profiles including central nervous
system depressants,
1a and bradycardic 1b and antitumoral 1c
agents. Specifically, cyclobutarenes, due to their structural
rigidity and high intrinsic energy of the strained cyclobutene
ring,
2 exhibit high reactivities and act as powerful and synthe-
tically useful building blocks. 3 As a result, such molecules were
widely applied in the assembly of various polycyclic scaﬀolds
through inter- and intramolecular Diels–Alder reactions,
with the key advance here involving the in situ generation of
ortho-xylylene intermediates upon thermal activation.
4 The
prominence of these cyclobutarenes has stimulated great
efforts to establish effective methods for their syntheses, with
these methods often including 1,4-elimination cycloaddition of
functionalized arenes,
5 Parham cyclization, 6 photo-induced
cycloadditions,7 thermal extrusion reactions, 8 intramolecular
addition of carbanions to benzynes, 9 [2+2+2] cycloadditions of
1,5-hexadiyne,10 ring expansion of cycloproparenes, 11 [2+2]
cycloadditions of allene precursors 12 and other methods. 13
However, most of the approaches so far developed rely on high
temperatures (400–800 1C), strong bases ( n-BuLi and NaNH
2),
and multiple steps, or suffer from a narrow substrate scope and
the need to carry out prefunctionalization of starting materials.
Therefore, facile and practical protocols are still needed to
synthesize cyclobutarenes and their derivatives from simple
precursors and inexpensive catalysts.
Eﬀective control of the chemoselectivity of the same reactants
toward the structural diversity via chemodivergent strategies
represents one of the extremely important tasks that could be
realized by changing the catalysts and other reaction
parameters.
14 Over the years, numerous chemodivergent
methods have been developed to establish molecular diversity
from readily available synthons.
15 Our group has presented
several chemodivergent reactions toward polycyclic rings with
bioactive importance, demonstrating high utility in skeletal
diversity.
16 To continue our interest in the design of chemodi-
vergent reactions by means of [2+2] cycloaddition of yne-
allenones (Scheme 1a),
17 we questioned whether catalytic
tunable silane-mediated conjugate reductions of yne-allenones
could be achieved by combining diverse reductive systems,
thereby levering a chemoselective entry to cyclobutarenes
(Scheme 1a). With this concept in mind, we conducted an
Fe(acac)
3-promoted reduction reaction between yne-allenones 1
and phenylsilane 2 in ethanol and found that the transformation
proceeded through a [2+2] cycloaddition/1,6-conjugate reduction
cascade, accessing 1,2-dihydrocyclobuta[ a]naphthalen-4-ols 3
with generally good yields (Scheme 1b). Interestingly,
exchanging the Fe–H complex for the Cu–H system resulted
in a mechanistically different reductive pathway to give
cyclobuta[a]naphthalene-4(2H)-ones 4 via a [2+2] cycloaddition/
1,4-conjugate transfer reduction sequence (Scheme 1c).
The current protocol represents the first combination of [2+2]
cycloaddition with conjugate reductions starting from
yne-allenones with silanes for the direct synthesis of new cyclo-
butarenes. Herein, we elaborate these catalytic chemodivergent
reactions.
Our initial investigation commenced with the treatment of
benzene-tethered yne-allenone 1a with PhSiH
3 (2a) and
Fe(acac)3 in a 1 : 1 : 2 mole ratio at 60 1C under Ar conditions
using ethanol (EtOH) as the reaction medium. The reduction
reaction proceeded to generate the target product 3a in 81%

yield (Table 1, entry1). Lowering the dosage of Fe(acac) 3 was not
beneficial for this transformation as lower yields of 3a were
observed (entries 2 and 3). In contrast, an increase in the
amount of Fe(acac) 3 to 2.5 equivalents did not improve the
eﬃciency of this reaction as well (entry 4). We then examined
other transition-metal salts such as Ru(acac)
3 and Co(acac) 2 to
evaluate this transformation, but both showed lower catalytic
performances in comparison with Fe(acac)
3 (entry 1 vs. entries
5 and 6). The subsequent screening of the reaction media
including methanol (CH
3OH) and tetrahydrofuran (THF)
revealed that the reaction could work in these solvents, but
gave lower yield than in EtOH (entry 1 vs. entries 7 and 8).
Decreasing or increasing the reaction temperature showed no
positive eﬀect on the yield of 3a (entries 9 and 10). Finally,
several other silanes such as Et
3SiH, Ph3SiH and polymethylhy-
drosiloxane (PMHS) were screened, showing that all these
reducing agents did not improve the yield of 3a (entries 11–13).
With these optimized conditions in hand, we set out to
systematically investigate the generality of this 1,6-conjugate
reduction by examining a set of yne-allenones with diﬀerent
substitution patterns. As shown in Scheme 2a, the influence of
substituents (R
1) in the arylalkynyl moiety of yne-allenones 1
was first evaluated. Substituents with diverse electronic and
steric characteristics were well accommodated, and products
3b–3i could be generated with comparable efficiency. Both
electron-rich (methyl, 1b–1c) and electron-poor (chloro, 1d–1e
bromo 1f, trifluoromethyl 1g and ester 1h) groups at different
positions can tolerate the reductive conditions well. Similarly,
2-thienyl analogue 1i still showed a high reactivity profile,
thus giving access to the corresponding 2-thienyl substituted
product 3i in 88% yield. Moreover, the electronic nature of
the internal arene ring of yne-allenones was also briefly
investigated. Various substituents such as methyl, methoxy,
fluoro and chloro were introduced in the C4 or C5 position of
the internal arene ring and these substrates were then reacted
with phenylsilane under the standard conditions. As antici-
pated, the reactions proceeded readily, enabling Fe-mediated
1,6-conjugate reduction entry to approach the corresponding
products 3j–3p in 45–81% yields. The Fe-mediated reductive
system can be easily amplified with a 4.0 mmol scale by
carrying out the reaction of 1a under the standard conditions
(70%, Scheme 2b).
To expand the utility of this methodology, we turned to
explore the feasibility of CuH-promoted conjugate reduction.

By using CuCN and a 1,1 0-bis(diphenylphosphino)ferrocene
(DPPF) ligand as a catalytic system, the reaction of 1a with
methyldimethoxysilane ( 2b, Me(MeO) 2SiH) in a 1 : 1.5 mole
ratio occurred smoothly in the presence of NaOMe in DCE at
50 1C under Ar conditions, and the unexpected dihydro-
cyclobuta[a]naphthalen-4(2H)-one 4a was selectively aﬀorded
in 90% yield (Table 2, entry 1). The preliminary results
prompted us to further search for the optimal conditions for
accessing product 4a. Several other copper salts including CuI,
CuBr and Cu(OAc)
2 were tried for this transformation, but all
these catalysts showed fairly lower catalytic abilities than CuCN
(entries 2–4 vs. entry 1). Afterward, the effect of the types of
silanes was probed, and the subsequent screening of other
silanes such as PhSiH
3,E t 3SiH and Ph 3SiH indicated that all
these silanes gave extremely unsatisfactory results (entries 5–7).
Having demonstrated the viability of engaging the yne-
allenone 1a in the chemodivergent reduction, we then
investigated the substrate scope of this protocol (Scheme 3).
At the outset, a variety of electron donating and withdrawing
substituents (such as methyl, ethyl, and chloro) were installed
into the phenyl ring relative to the alkynyl moiety of substrates
1 and in all the cases the desired products 4a–4g were obtained
with 70–90% yields. Moreover, 2-thienyl counterpart 1h was a
suitable surrogate for this transfer reduction ( 4h). Alternatively,
yne-allenones bearing various substituents (R
1) including
methyl, fluoro, and chloro at the C4 or C5 position of
the internal arene ring were compatible with Cu–H catalytic
conditions, furnishing dihydrocyclobuta[ a]naphthalen-4(2H)-
ones 4i–4m with yields ranging from 73% to 85%.
It is well-known that the combination of PhSiH
3 and
Fe(acac)3 would provide Fe( III)-hydride species (Fe IIILn–H),
which could release a hydrogen radical. For this reason, 2.0
equivalents of 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-1-piperidinyloxy (TEMPO) as
a radical scavenger were subjected to the reaction of 1a under
the Fe(
III)–H catalytic conditions (Scheme 4a). As expected, the
progress of the reaction was completely suppressed, revealing
that the reaction might include a hydrogen radical process.
In addition, when 2.0 equivalents of TEMPO were added into
the Cu-catalyzed system, the reaction could give product 4a in
79% yield, indicating that this process did not involve the
formation of a hydrogen radical (Scheme 4a).
On the basis of the above observations and literature
reports,
18 a reasonable mechanism for product 3 is proposed
in Scheme 4b. Initially, the Fe( III) complex reacts with phenyl-
silane in ethanol to give Fe( III)-hydride species, along with
ethyl(phenylsilyl)oxonium. Then, Fe( III)-hydride species is
trapped by cycloadduct A, generated from intramolecular
[2+2] cycloaddition of yne-allenones 1, thus leading to the
formation of intermediate B through 1,6-hydrogen radical
addition and the Fe( II) complex. Subsequently, single-electron
reduction between B and the Fe( II) complex gives the stabilized
naphthol anion C and regenerates the Fe( III) complex.

Intermediate C captures a proton from ethyl(phenylsilyl)
oxonium to provide the final products 3. In the formation of
products 4 (Scheme 5), the active Cu–H species, in situ-generated
from the reaction of CuCN with DPPF and hydrosilanes, is
intercepted by cycloadduct A from yne-allenones 1 to form a
p-complex D.19 Then, delivery of the hydride to the b-carbon
atom affords copper enolate intermediate E,w h i c hu n d e r g o e sa
s-bond metathesis with hydrosilanes, thus leading to intermedi-
ate F and regenerating catalytically active Cu–H species. Inter-
mediate F is converted into product 4 through desilicification by
the workup process. The reason for this chemodivergent reaction
depends on the difference in the catalytic abilities and modes
between Fe–H and Cu–H complexes.
In conclusion, starting from easily available yne-allenones and
hydrosilanes, new and tunable ca talytic [2+2] cycloaddition/
silane-mediated conjugate reductions were established for the first
time, enabling the direct construction of substituent-diverse cyclo-
butarenes with generally good yields. In the former, Fe–H species
enables a radical process to trigger 1,6-conjugate reduction to
dihydrocyclobuta[a]naphthalen-4-ols with good yields whereas the
latter generated new functionalized cyclobuta[a]naphthalen-4(2H)-
ones via 1,4-conjugate reduction by adopting the Cu–H complex as
the nucleophile. Both reductions show attractive advantages in
terms of the efficient control of chemoselectivity from the same
substrates and good compatibility with substituents, and thus
opens new approaches for the divergent synthesis of structurally
diverse cyclobuta[a]naphthalenes. Further investigation on their
asymmetric versions is currently underway in our laboratories.
